decisive_wording: B: "using a larger LLM as a judge on an EventBridge schedule and fine-tuning only when its scores move past a threshold" vs A: "a larger LLM grades its ratings ... when the grades shift past a threshold" vs C: "Built LLM-as-a-judge gating for a production Amazon Bedrock document-importance classifier"
info_preserved_or_lost: A and B keep the same facts: automated retraining, production Bedrock classifier, research documents rated by importance, larger LLM evaluating on an EventBridge schedule, threshold-gated fine-tuning. B also names the recognized 'LLM as a judge' pattern in plain phrasing. C adds an action verb ('Built') and the judge term, but drops 'research documents' (compressed to 'document-importance') and the explicit 'automated retraining' framing, and 'scores it' leaves unclear what is being scored.
credibility_change: All three describe a believable, interview-defensible mechanism. B and C use the standard 'LLM-as-a-judge' term, which a senior engineer will recognize at once. A's 'grades its ratings' is accurate but less idiomatic. C's 'gating' framing is precise but could be read as overclaiming a separate system.
readability_change: B reads as one natural sentence a recruiter can restate ('retrains a classifier only when a bigger model's scores shift'). A is about as readable, but the 'grades/ratings' wordplay adds a small parsing step. C is the hardest to read: it opens with a noun stack ('LLM-as-a-judge gating for a production Amazon Bedrock document-importance classifier') before the colon. B wins only narrowly over A, so the advantage is marginal.
